    I'll start this off with a random, weird thing that's happening right now:

    When we were rapidly expanding last year, I used my personal credit to rent out three houses for our employees because, even with the amount of money they were set to be making, they had no rental or credit history whatsoever, and a bunch of them couldn't pass background checks either.

    After the explosion last Spring, we asked to be allowed to terminate our leases early. Two of the landlords happily accommodated this, one of them even returning our full security deposit, even though people left those houses in frat-party condition.

    At the last house, however, there was a different issue. One of our employees - one of those prepper/minimalist types - decided to completely turn off the HVAC during the hot, humid Florida summer, resulting in a mold problem that we gladly and immediately paid to fix. 

    The landlord, unfortunately, is a cold-blooded attorney who now seems intent on using us to build a new addition on her house or something. She "agreed" to allow us to terminate the lease early after the mold issue was dealt with, under the clause that we'd be released from the lease once the house re-rented... but that was four months ago and the house hasn't even been listed with the agent she supposedly hired. It pretty much seems like she just wants us to pay full term for a house she knows we can't occupy.

    Long story short: think twice, three times, or more, before being a nice guy and using your credit and other assets to secure housing for people. Hire locals with existing housing arrangements whenever possible and avoid bringing roving bands of wannabe farmers in from wherever (like I did)... especially if they're coming without references 😬

    This was a comment made by Emma (not my wife) on Patreon in response to the mini-pod on re-centering the feminine in agriculture, and it was too good not to repost here:

    "My cousin used to work in DC, and he said they'd have a job description requiring 10 years of Russian speaking. A woman with only 7 years of experience wouldn't apply, but 8 dudes with 1-2 years or no experience would apply, and then that would be the pool of applicants they were left to choose from. 

    I wonder about the power in recruiting to address some of what you're saying here. Big  corporations have recruiting departments. I don't know football well, but they send out scouts to build a good team. 

    So many farms I know are so desperate for help they will take anyone who shows up, and especially anyone that sticks around. This summer I saw a posting in August by a local farm, "Now Hiring All Positions: good work ethic and competency is a plus. BEING ALIVE AND ABLE TO SHOW UP FOR WORK ARE THE ONLY REQUIREMENTS. Seriously, someone apply."

    Of the three farms that have hired me, only one asked for a resume and called my references, and that was the farm where I worked with the strongest team of people, women, I ever have.

    I think we need to change the common, and I'd say masculine, hiring system on farms from the "whoever shows up" model, to valuing workers who are thoughtful and care to show what they can and plan to bring to the team. 

    I wonder a lot about building a human resources department/consulting resource for farmers. This could be done by creating template job descriptions and applications, consulting, and a network to support referrals and references. This could also include guidance on creating job opportunities that are attractive to skilled workers, as well as a resource for workers to share their needs/experiences and find better opportunities.

    And! I think this is already happening here between the discord network, zoom meetings, and template sharing. It would be interesting to have a sort of farm-specific LinkedIn space connected to the software being discussed on discord, not sure if one already exists or if this conversation is already happening (if so, please send me there!). 

    If there were a database that farmers could check when they needed to hire someone new, they could post the job but also reach out to the local experienced farmworkers, or specific people if the job really aligns with their experience, and let them know about the opportunity. That person might not always be available, but they might be able to refer someone else they've worked with. Instead of just hoping the next person who thinks they want to farm is actually competent enough to farm..

    A long comment, but this is where my mind goes when it comes to switching to more feminine structures in the decision making on farms."

    Hey everyone, thanks to everyone that made it to yesterday's roundtable. Here's the link to the video: https://youtu.be/aBcD12EfG3H

    Key takeaways (for me, at least):

    1.) Most negative experiences co-ops and collectives revolve around interpersonal issues. These included unfair distribution of duties; the amount of time that it took to resolve interpersonal problems (fear of and disdain for meetings, lack of communication, etc.), blocs and groups within collectives - ranging from friend circles to nepotism - derailing the ability to communicate and operate in good faith; wide variability in experience and commitment levels

    2.) Some of the key characteristics of cooperatives that work well include 1.) taking the time to go slowly, especially in the creation of bylaws, governance, and modes of communication, 2.) forming cooperatives from people who already have a fairly long history of working together, 3.) very detailed delineation of roles, responsibilities, and metrics for evaluating performance objectively, 4.) communication that reinforces affirmation; explicitly and consistently acknowledging the good in each member of the team so that people feel that their contributions are understood, recognized, and not taken for granted, 5.) an emphasis on training, both technical and cultural, so that everyone joining the collective/co-op knows the rules of the road and everyone's operating on the same set of principles, 6.) a fairly long buy-in period, including a monetary component, to ensure that everyone actually has skin in the game and something to lose (besides clout, which was also raised as an issue)

    3.) A common thread that seemed to lead to interpersonal issues were farmers experiencing success in their individual enterprises, and wanting to "share the wealth" with others as quickly as possible; an intoxicating excitement around working with other people that causes us, in our haste, to choose the wrong people to work with and/or fail to create the organizational systems/processes to manage personalities, expectations, etc.

    Some of patterns for building successful collaborations included:

    1.) Starting slowly by beginning informally - find ways to work together with others without getting "married." Date awhile, work some things out, and see who you actually want to be in a long term relationship with

    2.) The nucleus of new collaborations should be proven operators, not wannabes

    3.) Establishing patterns of communication, especially in the early stages, is arguably more important than work products, deliverables, and "progress." Bylaws and governance can emerge from patterns established in item 1, so that creating these becomes a natural exercise instead of a bureaucratic nightmare

    4.) Standards - operational, product, communication, cultural - are extremely important, as is the need to develop training and documentation around them. Early collaborations need to focus hard on developing their culture, documenting the parts that work, discarding the parts that don't, and ensuring that new entrants to the collaboration demonstrate an affinity toward that culture (and quickly closing the door on candidates that don't)

    Wow, so good... major thanks to everyone for being so vulnerable, sharing your stories and asking hard questions! 

    I apologize for the length, but the recurring theme of interpersonal dynamics/conflict resolution brought up a practice that we include in our weekly meetings that I want to share incase it might help or spark helpful conversation:

    This practice is something we call "story checks", which is essentially a safe space to bring up potential resentment, guilt or misunderstanding that has been building. The idea is to present the issue as a story that you've been telling yourself (ie. "I'm not doing enough and so‐and-so is mad at me", or "I'm doing more than so-and-so because they are lazy" etc.) and present it as a personal feeling/perception that may or may not be true (thus a "story", rather than an accusation) and to then come to a conclusion of a "shared story" with the others involved, hearing their personal stories and perceptions as well (treating it as a problem to be solved together, not me vs. them). It could be that the presented "story" was just a false perception, or it could have some truth to it, and regardless the goal is to clear the air and if necessary decide on some tangible adjustments (in perception and/or action). 

    Ie. it could be true that so-and-so wasn't working as hard, but because they were going through something, not just out of laziness. Therefore some forgiveness, as well as a plan for them to ease back into action or some of their roles to be reassigned could be the takeaway (look for systemic issues as well, like could be a sign of burn-out culture). Of course, it could also be true that they are working less than they should (based on previously agreed upon expectations), in which case, rather than simply accusing them of being lazy and telling then to step it up, look for a solution to the problem. Maybe they haven't been trained well enough, maybe it's not the right position for them, etc. and form a new agreement. 
    Also, an essential part of this exercise is everyone committing to full honesty, and to trust in others honesty, otherwise new "stories" might form in the moment that others are holding back or have alterior motives, etc.

Ok, so a month later here's the response to this (tagging @everyone because I think it's important)

"Metrics are different for bipoc folks"
-False.

Metrics are metrics, and most of us are arguably more obsessed with them than White folks are because the stakes are higher: resources dedicated to equity are 1.) hard to get (in terms of both time and money), and 2.) have a lot of work to do, so the serious among us are pretty determined to ensure we aren't wasting anything. We have to be twice as good to get half as much, and are rarely allowed to fail more than once, so we're very big on goal-setting, establishing KPIs, and auditing progress against them relentlessly.

There are exceptions to this, usually among newer efforts led by younger people, but you'll rarely find them reacting with hostility toward goalsetting and metrics. It'll usually just be a matter of pragmatism. For example when I brought this up with City Food Storage during their Earthship story, Jordan didn't get defensive about it and say "metrics are different for Black folks." It was instead more of a technical/practical issue: "it's hard to establish the number of people using the fridges and how much food they're taking without setting up a pseudo-surveillance system that may disincentivize people from using the fridges... but we'd love to figure out how to make this work."

There's nothing wrong with doing foundational work e.g. building partnerships and gathering wisdom, etc., but there's also nothing wrong with asking "what's it all for?"  considering that many justice/equity-oriented" non-profits end up in the business of self-perpetuation and, as a result, end up making resources unavailable to measurable forward progress. To be sure, non-profits CAN serve an instrumental role in making that progress happens, but many non-profits simply don't because they don't know how... this is especially true of NGOs built as an off-ramp by people that failed to make a go at commercial ag.

The key difference between White and non-White (esp. Indigenous) people in these spaces isn't goalsetting and metrics... but rather speed. White people tend to want to move fast and break things while BIPOC are usually more careful and deliberate around how, where, and if to move; this is something I've exhibited here at Earthship that's frustrated the hell out of a lot of White people. This difference is both cultural (it's hard to keep reciprocity and people-relationships in balance at high speed) and practical (see above: our mistakes have harsher consequences than White folks' mistakes, so we're prone to be very careful about making and executing decisions).

But all in all, no I don't think you were out of life asking the questions you did, especially since those questions were solicited. 

Hope that helps.
